computers.title: Computers
computers.subtitle: Servers and virtual machines {name} can work on, besides this one.
computers.load_failed: The computer list could not be loaded. Is the backend running?
computers.add_subtitle: Choose where the computer lives. You can add as many as you like.
computers.remove_confirm: Remove “{computer}” from {name}? The computer itself keeps running; {name} just stops connecting to it.
computers.remove_destroy_vm: Also delete the virtual machine and its disk from this computer
computers.welcome_body: Connect a server you rent, import one from your hosting account, or let {name} create a virtual machine right here. Every machine is reached the same safe way: over SSH, with a key only {name} holds.
computers.how_1_body: Type an address, pick a server from your hosting account, or create a local VM.
computers.how_2_body: A password is used once to plant {name}’s own key, then forgotten.
computers.how_3_body: {name} pins each server’s identity and warns you if it ever changes.
computers.path_server_body: Any VPS or machine you can reach over SSH — Hostinger, Strato, IONOS, a Raspberry Pi at home.
computers.path_server_lead: Enter the address and login your hosting provider gave you.
computers.path_cloud_body: Connect Hostinger, Hetzner or DigitalOcean once and pick servers from a list — no IPs to copy.
computers.path_cloud_lead: {name} reads your server list with an API token you create at your provider.
computers.path_local_body: {name} creates a fresh Ubuntu computer inside this one — a safe sandbox to try things in.
computers.path_local_lead: An isolated Ubuntu machine on this computer, powered by Multipass.
computers.field_host_hint: You find it in your provider’s panel, for example “203.0.113.10”.
computers.login_once_body: {name} logs in once, adds its own key and forgets the password. The safest choice.
computers.login_key_body: You pasted {name}’s public key into your provider’s panel or the server’s authorized_keys.
computers.login_keep_body: The password is stored in your system’s keychain. Works, but a key is safer.
computers.password_once_hint: Used only for this one login. It is never saved.
computers.password_keep_hint: Stored encrypted in your system’s keychain, never in a file.
computers.key_paste_hint: {name}’s public key — paste it into your provider’s SSH-key settings
computers.token_body: {name} needs an API token to list your servers. It only reads the list — and on Hostinger adds {name}’s key to the server you pick.
computers.token_paste: Create a token, copy it and paste it here.
computers.token_storage: The token is stored in your system’s keychain and only ever sent to your provider.
computers.no_servers_in_account: This account has no servers yet.
computers.auto_key_body: {name} adds its own key to this server through {provider}. It can take a minute until the server accepts it.
computers.local_checking: Looking for Multipass on this computer…
computers.local_missing_body: Multipass is Canonical’s free, open-source tool that runs Ubuntu virtual machines on Windows, macOS and Linux. {name} uses it to create and manage your local VMs.
computers.local_missing_foot: On Windows it needs Hyper-V (Windows Pro) or VirtualBox. After installing, click “Check again”.
computers.vm_name_invalid: Use 2–40 lowercase letters, digits or hyphens, starting with a letter.
computers.local_key_note: The VM starts with {name}’s key already inside. No password is ever created.
computers.fix_auth_body: Enter the password once and {name} adds its own key — the password is not saved.
computers.fix_hostkey_body: That happens when a server is reinstalled — or when someone pretends to be it. {name} stopped connecting. Only trust the new identity if you rebuilt the server yourself.
computers.trust_new_identity: I reinstalled it — trust the new identity
computers.facts_empty: Facts appear after the first successful check.
computers.auth_key_body: {name} logs in with its key. No password is stored anywhere.
computers.auth_password_body: The password sits in your system’s keychain. Install {name}’s key to drop it.
computers.console_empty: Run a command on this computer. Press ↑ for earlier ones.
computers.console_placeholder: Type a command and press Enter
computers.console_offline: The console is available while the computer is online
computers.identity_body: One key for all your computers. Paste it into a provider panel to let {name} in without a password.
computers.ready_body: IDE sessions and agents that run here need tmux, git and a logged-in coding CLI. They then keep working while this PC is off.
computers.ready_offline: Check the computer first; this list is read over SSH.
computers.ready_copy_login_hint: Copies this computer's login file for this CLI to the server. Only do this on a server you own.
computers.ready_login_copied: {agent} is now logged in on the server.
computers.ready_needs_root: Needs root or sudo on this login.
computers.ready_body_windows: IDE sessions and agents that run on this Windows computer need Git for Windows and a logged-in coding CLI. There they stop when this PC disconnects.
computers.ready_needs_admin: Needs an administrator login on this computer.
computers.keep_title: Keep working when this PC closes
computers.keep_body: When you quit the app, running Agentic IDE sessions move to this computer with their folder and conversation, and carry on there.
computers.keep_failed: The setting could not be saved.
computers.keep_windows_note: Windows computers are not offered here: agents there stop when this PC disconnects.
computers.empty_body: Connect a server you rent or a machine at home, and {name} and its agents can work there — even while this PC is off.
computers.empty_foot: Hostinger, Hetzner, DigitalOcean, IONOS, a Raspberry Pi or any server with SSH.
computers.auth_private_key_body: A key you already use. It is kept in your system's keychain.
computers.access_key_via_login: {name} uses the current login once to install its own key, then switches over.
computers.access_identities_body: The server's fingerprint proves it is the same machine every time. {name}'s public key is what the server trusts.
computers.access_no_fingerprint: The server's identity is recorded on the first successful connection.
computers.wz_local_sub: A fresh Ubuntu machine, powered by Multipass
computers.wz_no_match: No provider matches. Pick “Other server” to connect any machine with SSH.
computers.wz_m_api_body: Pick the server from your {provider} account — no address to copy.
computers.wz_m_api_body_keys: Pick the server from your {provider} account; {name} adds its key for you, no password needed.
computers.wz_m_password_body: {name} logs in once, installs its own key and forgets the password.
computers.wz_m_private_key_body: Use a key you already log in with. It stays in your system's keychain.
computers.wz_m_jarvis_key_body: Add {name}'s public key in {provider} yourself — no password ever typed here.
computers.wz_keep_password: Keep using the password instead of a key
computers.wz_private_key_hint: Paste the key, or choose the file (often ~/.ssh/id_ed25519).
computers.wz_key_file_too_big: That file is too large to be an SSH key.
computers.wz_passphrase_placeholder: Only if the key has one
computers.wz_open_key_page: Open the SSH key page at {provider}
computers.wz_fix_auth: Check the login name and password or key. On many servers the login is root.
computers.wz_fix_unreachable: Check the address and that the server is switched on. The SSH port is usually 22.
computers.wz_fix_timeout: The server did not answer. A firewall may block SSH, or the address is wrong.
computers.wz_fix_host_key_changed: This address answered with a different identity than before. Only continue if you reinstalled the server.
computers.wz_fix_protocol: The server did not speak SSH as expected. Check the port.
computers.wz_fix_bad_key: The key could not be read. Paste the private key (not the .pub file) and check the passphrase.
computers.wz_pick_server: Pick a server from your {provider} account
computers.wz_next_agents: Get it ready for coding agents
computers.wz_next_agents_body: Checks tmux, git and the coding CLIs, and installs what is missing on one click.
computers.wz_next_ide_body: In the Agentic IDE, choose “Runs on: {computer}” when you open a workspace.
computers.cx_subtitle: Enter the address. {name} logs in with this PC's SSH keys or asks for what is missing, and tests the connection before it saves anything.
computers.cx_address_hint: The IP your provider shows, e.g. 203.0.113.10 — or paste a whole "ssh root@…" line.
computers.cx_password_hint: Used once: {name} adds its own key and forgets the password.
computers.cx_private_key_hint: Paste it or pick the file (for example id_ed25519). It stays in your system's keychain.
computers.cx_key_too_big: That file is too large to be an SSH key.
computers.cx_own_key_hint: {name}'s public key — it must already be in the server's authorized_keys
computers.cx_key_already_there: {name}'s key is already on the server
computers.cx_keep_password: Keep the password instead of installing {name}'s key
computers.cx_accounts_body: See all your servers in one list and pick one — no IP to copy.
computers.cx_vm_link: Create a virtual machine on this PC instead
computers.cx_fail_auth: The server refused the login. Check the password, the key or the login name.
computers.cx_fail_unreachable: The server could not be reached. Check the address and that SSH (port 22) is open.
computers.cx_fail_timeout: The server did not answer in time. Check the address and your firewall.
computers.cx_fail_host_key_changed: The server's identity changed since the last connection.
computers.cx_fail_bad_key: This does not look like a valid private key, or the passphrase is wrong.
computers.cx_paste_hint: An IP or host name, like 203.0.113.10. A whole “ssh user@host” line works too.
computers.cx_key_own_body: A private key you already use for this server.
computers.cx_key_assistant_body: You add {name}'s public key to the server once.
computers.cx_key_assistant_hint: Add it to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server, or in your hosting panel under “SSH keys”. Then press Connect.
computers.cx_key_from_paste: Using the private key from the address box.
computers.cx_agent_step2: On that computer, paste them into Claude Code, Codex or another coding agent. It turns on SSH and adds {name}'s key.
computers.cx_agent_step3: The agent ends with one line that starts with JARVIS-CONNECT. Paste that line into “Server address” above.
computers.cx_agent_done: The agent's line is in: {name}'s key is on that computer. Press Connect.
computers.cx_connect_hint: Nothing is saved until the test works.
computers.cx_check_failed: The connection does not work yet
computers.cx_step_probe_warn: Logged in, but the test command gave no answer. The connection still works.
computers.cx_step_save_warn: Saved, but the follow-up check did not come back online.
computers.cx_verified_body: {name} reached it, logged in and ran a test command.
computers.cx_auto_hint: {name} tries the SSH keys this PC already uses. If none of them opens the server, it asks for the password once.
computers.cx_ask_password: None of this PC's SSH keys opens this server. Enter its password once: {name} then sets up its own key and forgets the password.
computers.cx_key_only_title: This server only lets in keys it knows
computers.cx_key_only_body: Run this line once on the server, in your hosting panel's web console or any SSH session. It adds {name}'s key. Then press Try again.
computers.cx_key_only_agent: Or let a coding agent on the server do it
